meta.notes: Solo questions: 9 per character (3 easy/3 medium/3 hard) x10 characters = 90. Combo questions: 5 Duo Challenges (friend+own sidekick) + 5 Crew Combos (two friends) = 10. Correct combo answers award XP to both entities involved.

easy.rhyme: DJs use two turntables side by side, spinning records with musical pride.
easy.fact: DJs typically use two turntables (or decks) to mix music.
easy.q: How many turntables does a DJ usually use to mix?

easy.rhyme: The word 'space' can mean the room around you too, not just the stars up in the blue.
easy.fact: ‘Space’ can refer to physical space or area, not only outer space.
easy.q: Besides outer space, what else can the word "space" mean?
options: Empty area or room around you

easy.rhyme: Turn the volume knob up, the volume knob down, that changes how loud or soft the sound.
easy.fact: A volume knob controls how loud or soft sound is.
easy.q: What does a volume knob control?

medium.rhyme: Up, down, left, right, forward, back — six directions, that's the track!
medium.fact: Space around us has six basic directions of movement.
medium.q: How many directions can you move in space?

medium.rhyme: Sound needs air to shake and swing — in true space silence, it can't ring!
medium.fact: Sound waves need molecules (like air) to travel — they can't cross empty space.
medium.q: Can sound travel through a total vacuum?

medium.rhyme: Every star's a sun so bright — our own sun gives us day and light.
medium.fact: Every star you see is a distant sun, just like ours.
medium.q: What is a star, basically?

hard.rhyme: A DJ blends two songs into one smooth ride, matching the beats so they never collide.
hard.fact: DJs use “beatmatching” to line up the tempo of two tracks.
hard.q: What's it called when a DJ matches the tempo of two songs?

hard.rhyme: Six directions meet at a single spot — that center point's the origin, believe it or not!
hard.fact: In spatial terms, the point where all directions meet is called the origin.
hard.q: What's the name for the point where all six directions meet?

hard.rhyme: Crossfaders slide the sound side to side, blending two tracks like a DJ's guide.
hard.fact: A crossfader lets a DJ blend audio between two turntables or channels.
hard.q: What tool lets a DJ blend sound between two turntables?

easy.rhyme: Air is all around, though it's hard to see, it fills up the space from the ground to a tree.
easy.fact: Air is invisible but present everywhere around us.
easy.q: Can you usually see air?

easy.rhyme: MCs use a microphone to make their voice loud, so their rhymes can reach the whole crowd.
easy.fact: Microphones amplify a voice so a crowd can hear it.
easy.q: What tool helps an MC's voice reach a big crowd?

easy.rhyme: Take a breath in, then let it out slow — that's how your lungs help your body go.
easy.fact: Lungs bring air in and out of the body.
easy.q: What body part do you breathe air into?

medium.rhyme: Breathe in deep, let your rhymes flow — air fuels the fire in your vocal show!
medium.fact: Breath control from your lungs powers your voice.
medium.q: What powers the sound of your voice?

medium.rhyme: Wind is just air on the run — pushed by heat from our big sun.
medium.fact: Wind happens when the sun heats air unevenly, so it moves around.
medium.q: What mainly causes wind?

medium.rhyme: Layers stack up, thin to thick — our atmosphere's a five-layer trick.
medium.fact: Earth's atmosphere is made of several stacked layers.
medium.q: Is Earth's atmosphere made of layers?

hard.rhyme: MCs freestyle rhymes right off the top, making up bars before they stop.
hard.fact: Freestyling is improvising rhymes on the spot, without prewritten lyrics.
hard.q: What's it called when an MC makes up rhymes on the spot?

hard.rhyme: Air pressure pushes on you all day, even though you don't feel it, it's here to stay.
hard.fact: Atmospheric air pressure constantly presses on us, though we don't usually notice it.
hard.q: Is there air pressure pushing on you all the time, even if you can't feel it?

hard.rhyme: A rhyme scheme's the pattern of rhymes in a song, like AABB, and it don't take long!
hard.fact: A rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhyming lines in lyrics, like AABB.
hard.q: What do we call the pattern of rhymes in a song?

easy.rhyme: Fire feels warm, and it glows bright with light, that's heat and light put together — quite a sight!
easy.fact: Fire produces both heat and light.
easy.q: What two things does fire give off?

easy.rhyme: Graffiti artists use spray cans with care, to paint big bold letters up in the air.
easy.fact: Graffiti art is often made using spray paint.
easy.q: What tool do graffiti artists often use?

easy.rhyme: Never touch a flame, it's much too hot, always ask a grown-up, that's a smart thought!
easy.fact: Fire safety: never touch flames, and ask an adult for help around fire.
easy.q: What should you do if you see a fire?

medium.rhyme: Fire needs three: heat, fuel, air — take one away, the flame's not there!
medium.fact: A fire needs heat, fuel, and oxygen — the ‘fire triangle.’
medium.q: Which is NOT one of the three things fire needs?

medium.rhyme: Red flame's warm, but blue's more hot — color tells you what heat's got.
medium.fact: Flame color is a clue to temperature — blue flames burn hotter than red ones.
medium.q: Which flame color is usually hotter?

medium.rhyme: Spray paint's pigment mixed with gas, pushed out fast by pressure — pass!
medium.fact: Spray cans use pressurized gas to push pigment out in a fine mist.
medium.q: What pushes the paint out of a spray can?

hard.rhyme: A mural's a big painting on a wall, telling a story that's seen by all.
hard.fact: A mural is a large piece of artwork painted directly on a wall.
hard.q: What do we call a big painting made directly on a wall?

hard.rhyme: Fire needs fuel to keep burning strong, without it the flame won't last very long.
hard.fact: Fuel is required to sustain a fire, as part of the fire triangle.
hard.q: What happens to a fire if it runs out of fuel?

hard.rhyme: Stencils help artists repeat a design, tracing the same shape again and in line.
hard.fact: Stencils are used in art (including graffiti) to repeat a design precisely.
hard.q: What tool helps an artist repeat the exact same shape?

easy.rhyme: The ground beneath you is solid and still, that's the earth, from the valley to the hill.
easy.fact: Earth (the ground) is generally solid beneath us.
easy.q: What do we call the solid ground beneath our feet?

easy.rhyme: Breaking is a dance with spins and flips, done to a beat with quick footwork tips.
easy.fact: Breaking (breakdancing) involves spins, flips, and fast footwork.
easy.q: What is "breaking"?

easy.rhyme: Stretch before you dance, nice and slow, that helps your muscles bend and go.
easy.fact: Stretching helps prepare muscles for movement.
easy.q: Why do dancers stretch before dancing?
options: To help their muscles move better

medium.rhyme: Gravity pulls you to the floor — that's why you spin, then rise for more.
medium.fact: Gravity pulls everything toward the ground.
medium.q: What pulls a b-boy back down after a jump?

medium.rhyme: Friction grips your sneaker sole — helps you freeze and hold control.
medium.fact: Friction between your shoes and the floor is what lets you grip and freeze.
medium.q: What lets your sneakers grip the floor?

medium.rhyme: Muscles pull on bones like strings — that's the power a b-boy's body brings.
medium.fact: Muscles pull on bones, through tendons, to create movement.
medium.q: What do muscles pull on to create movement?

hard.rhyme: A 'freeze' in breaking holds the pose in place, balancing still with style and grace.
hard.fact: A “freeze” is a breaking move where the dancer holds a balanced pose.
hard.q: What's it called when a b-boy or b-girl holds a still balanced pose?

hard.rhyme: Earth's crust is the thin outer shell we stand on, way below is a hot core it's built upon.
hard.fact: Earth has an outer crust, with hotter layers (mantle and core) beneath it.
hard.q: What is the outer layer of the Earth called?

hard.rhyme: Momentum keeps a spin going strong, the faster you turn, the more it lasts long.
hard.fact: Momentum helps sustain spinning motion — more speed means more momentum.
hard.q: What helps keep a dancer's spin going?

easy.rhyme: Water can be liquid, ice, or steam, three different forms of the same team.
easy.fact: Water exists in three states: liquid, solid (ice), and gas (steam or vapor).
easy.q: Which of these is a form of water?

easy.rhyme: Reading books fills your brain with facts, that's how knowledge grows and stays intact.
easy.fact: Reading builds knowledge.
easy.q: What's one great way to gain knowledge?

easy.rhyme: Rivers flow downhill to the sea, carrying water endlessly.
easy.fact: Rivers generally flow downhill toward larger bodies of water like the sea.
easy.q: Which way do rivers usually flow?

medium.rhyme: Water rises, turns to steam, falls as rain — it's a cycle theme.
medium.fact: The water cycle: evaporation, condensation, then precipitation.
medium.q: What comes after water evaporates into the sky?

medium.rhyme: Ice floats high 'cause it's less dense — that's frozen water's one defense.
medium.fact: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
medium.q: Why does ice float on water?
options: It's less dense than liquid water

medium.rhyme: Knowledge flows like water clear — wisdom passed from ear to ear.
medium.fact: Knowledge, like water, moves and spreads when it's shared.
medium.q: What's one way knowledge is passed along, just like water flows?

hard.rhyme: Water covers most of our Earth's face, about seventy percent of the whole place!
hard.fact: Roughly 70% of Earth's surface is covered by water.
hard.q: About how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?

hard.rhyme: A hypothesis is a guess you can test, using science to see which idea is best.
hard.fact: A hypothesis is a testable explanation or prediction in the scientific method.
hard.q: What do scientists call a testable guess?

hard.rhyme: Salt water and fresh water aren't the same, oceans are salty, rivers are plain.
hard.fact: Oceans are saltwater; most rivers and lakes are freshwater.
hard.q: Which is saltier, the ocean or a river?

easy.rhyme: Bats sleep upside down through the day, then wake at night to swoop and play.
easy.fact: Bats are nocturnal and often sleep hanging upside down during the day.
easy.q: When are bats usually most active?

easy.rhyme: Sound travels in waves, moving through the air, until it reaches your ear with care.
easy.fact: Sound travels through air in waves.
easy.q: How does sound usually travel to your ears?

easy.rhyme: A drum makes a boom when you give it a hit, that's vibration — sound's favorite bit.
easy.fact: Sound is created by vibration.
easy.q: What makes the sound when you hit a drum?

medium.rhyme: Bats send out sound that bounces back — that's echolocation, nature's sound hack.
medium.fact: Bats use echolocation, bouncing sound waves off objects to find their way in the dark.
medium.q: How do bats ‘see’ in the dark?

medium.rhyme: Your ear catches sound waves, sends them to your brain, so you can hear a song's whole refrain.
medium.fact: Ears convert sound waves into signals your brain can understand.
medium.q: What does your ear turn sound waves into?

medium.rhyme: Louder sounds carry more energy through the air — that's why a shout travels further than a whisper's care.
medium.fact: Louder sounds have more energy, which is part of why they travel further.
medium.q: Which travels further, a shout or a whisper?

hard.rhyme: Bats aren't blind, that old idea's wrong — most bats can see, they've had eyesight all along.
hard.fact: The phrase "blind as a bat" is a myth — most bats can see just fine.
hard.q: Is it true that bats are actually blind?

hard.rhyme: Pitch is how high or low a sound may be, a tiny mouse squeaks in a pitch quite high, you see.
hard.fact: Pitch describes how high or low a sound is.
hard.q: What do we call how high or low a sound is?

hard.rhyme: Sound moves slower than a beam of light, that's why thunder booms after lightning's bright.
hard.fact: Sound travels much slower than light, which is why thunder is heard after lightning is seen.
hard.q: Why do we usually see lightning before we hear thunder?

easy.rhyme: A hug feels warm, a poke feels quick, both are touch — that's a body trick.
easy.fact: Touch includes many sensations, like pressure and warmth.
easy.q: Is a hug an example of touch?

easy.rhyme: Bees buzz from flower to flower each day, collecting pollen along the way.
easy.fact: Bees collect pollen while moving between flowers.
easy.q: What do bees collect from flowers?

easy.rhyme: Your fingertips are extra good at feeling things, more sensitive than your elbows or knees, they bring.
easy.fact: Fingertips have a high concentration of touch receptors, more sensitive than many other body parts.
easy.q: Which is usually more sensitive to touch, your fingertips or your elbow?

medium.rhyme: Bees feel the world through tiny hairs, sensing the wind and vibrations in the air.
medium.fact: Bees have tiny sensory hairs that detect touch, vibration, and airflow.
medium.q: What do bees use to sense touch and vibration?

medium.rhyme: Your skin's your biggest sense of all — it feels a touch, whether gentle or a rough footfall.
medium.fact: Skin is the body's largest organ, and it's covered in touch receptors.
medium.q: What is the body's largest touch-sensing organ?

medium.rhyme: Touch signals race from fingertip to brain, arriving in a flash, again and again.
medium.fact: Touch signals travel quickly through nerves from your skin to your brain.
medium.q: Where do touch signals travel to from your skin?

hard.rhyme: Nerve endings in skin send signals with speed, that's how you feel a touch you might need.
hard.fact: Nerve endings in the skin detect touch and send signals to the brain.
hard.q: What in your skin detects touch?

hard.rhyme: Bees can sense the buzz of their hive-mates near, using vibration instead of an ear.
hard.fact: Bees can sense vibrations, which helps with communication, like the waggle dance.
hard.q: What can bees sense to help them communicate?

hard.rhyme: Some receptors sense pressure and stretch — that's how your skin can tell a tight or loose belt.
hard.fact: Different touch receptors in skin detect different things, like pressure and stretch.
hard.q: Can your skin have different receptors for different kinds of touch, like pressure vs. stretch?

easy.rhyme: Your pupil gets bigger in a dark room, letting more light in to help vision bloom.
easy.fact: Pupils dilate (get bigger) in low light to let in more light.
easy.q: What happens to your pupils in a dark room?

easy.rhyme: Cats have whiskers that help them feel space, not just their eyes that see a face.
easy.fact: Cat whiskers help them sense their surroundings.
easy.q: What do cat whiskers help a cat sense?

easy.rhyme: Rainbows show colors when light bends through rain, red, orange, yellow, green — a colorful chain.
easy.fact: Rainbows form when light bends (refracts) through raindrops, showing colors.
easy.q: What causes a rainbow to appear?

medium.rhyme: Cat eyes catch the tiniest light — that's why they see so well at night.
medium.fact: Cats' eyes are specially adapted to see well in low light.
medium.q: Why can cats see well at night?
options: Their eyes catch tiny amounts of light
They don't actually see at night

medium.rhyme: Your eye has a part that bends the light just right, focusing what you see, day or night.
medium.fact: The lens in your eye focuses light onto the retina so you can see clearly.
medium.q: What part of your eye focuses light?

medium.rhyme: Two eyes see two views side by side — your brain blends them for depth, deep and wide.
medium.fact: Having two eyes gives you binocular vision, which helps you judge depth and distance.
medium.q: What does having two eyes help you judge?

hard.rhyme: The retina's a layer inside your eye, catching the light as it comes passing by.
hard.fact: The retina is the layer at the back of the eye that captures light.
hard.q: What part of the eye captures light at the back?

hard.rhyme: Cats have a special layer that reflects light back, that's why their eyes glow in the dark — no lack!
hard.fact: Cats have a reflective layer (tapetum lucidum) that makes their eyes appear to glow in low light.
hard.q: What causes a cat's eyes to seem to glow in the dark?
options: A reflective layer in their eyes

hard.rhyme: Color blindness means some colors mix and blend, that's a difference some people's eyes attend.
hard.fact: Color blindness is a condition where a person has difficulty distinguishing certain colors.
hard.q: What is color blindness?
options: Not being able to see at all

easy.rhyme: Your nose can smell a cookie baking sweet, that's your sense of smell — quite a treat!
easy.fact: Smell lets you detect scents, like food.
easy.q: Which body part do you smell with?

easy.rhyme: Wolves live and hunt together in a pack, working as a team, that's their knack.
easy.fact: Wolves are social animals that live in packs.
easy.q: Do wolves usually live alone or in packs?

easy.rhyme: Some smells warn you, like smoke in the air, that's your nose helping you take care.
easy.fact: Smell can serve as a warning sense, like detecting smoke.
easy.q: Can your sense of smell help warn you of danger, like smoke?

medium.rhyme: A wolf can smell a scent from a mile away — that nose can track a trail all day.
medium.fact: Wolves have an extraordinarily strong sense of smell.
medium.q: Which sense is a wolf especially famous for?

medium.rhyme: Smells sneak in through your nose so neat — tiny particles floating, invisible and fleet.
medium.fact: Smelling works by detecting tiny particles that float through the air.
medium.q: What floats through the air for your nose to detect?

medium.rhyme: Smell and taste are teammates in your head — that's why a stuffy nose dulls your bread.
medium.fact: Smell and taste work closely together to create the sense of flavor.
medium.q: Which other sense works closely with smell to create flavor?

hard.rhyme: A wolf's nose has way more smell receptors than yours, that's why their sniffing outperforms, of course!
hard.fact: Wolves (like dogs) have far more scent receptors than humans, giving them a much stronger sense of smell.
hard.q: Do wolves generally have a stronger sense of smell than humans?

hard.rhyme: Smell receptors line the top of your nose, sending signals wherever a scent goes.
hard.fact: Olfactory (smell) receptors are located inside the nasal cavity.
hard.q: Where are your smell receptors mainly located?

hard.rhyme: Some animals mark their space with scent, that's called scent-marking, a wild intent.
hard.fact: Many animals, including wolves, use scent marking to communicate territory.
hard.q: What is it called when an animal uses smell to mark its territory?

easy.rhyme: Sour candy makes your face scrunch tight, that's your taste buds reacting right.
easy.fact: Sour is one of the basic tastes detected by taste buds.
easy.q: What taste might make your face scrunch up?

easy.rhyme: Frogs live both in water and on land, that's why we call them amphibians, understand?
easy.fact: Frogs are amphibians, living both in water and on land.
easy.q: What kind of animal is a frog?

easy.rhyme: Your tongue can taste sweet things like a treat, that's one of the tastes your taste buds meet.
easy.fact: Sweet is one of the basic tastes.
easy.q: Is sweet one of the basic tastes your tongue can detect?

medium.rhyme: Your tongue has tiny bumps called taste buds bright — they sense sweet, salty, sour, bitter, quite a delight.
medium.fact: Your tongue is covered in taste buds that detect different tastes, like sweet, salty, sour, and bitter.
medium.q: What are the tiny bumps on your tongue that sense flavor called?

medium.rhyme: A frog's tongue flicks out fast as a wink, snapping up bugs quicker than you'd think.
medium.fact: Frogs use their long, quick tongues to catch prey.
medium.q: How does a frog usually catch its food?
options: By waiting for it to fall in its mouth

medium.rhyme: Taste buds refresh and renew every couple weeks — that's why new flavors are never far as it seeks.
medium.fact: Taste buds regenerate, typically renewing every couple of weeks.
medium.q: Do taste buds regenerate over time?

hard.rhyme: Umami's a taste that's savory and deep, found in foods like broth and cheese we keep.
hard.fact: Umami is a savory taste, one of the five basic tastes.
hard.q: What do we call the savory taste found in foods like broth and cheese?

hard.rhyme: A frog's skin can soak up water nearby — that's how they drink, no cup, don't ask why.
hard.fact: Frogs can absorb water through their skin instead of drinking with a mouth.
hard.q: How do frogs mostly take in water?

hard.rhyme: Taste and smell work as a team you see, that's why foods taste different when your nose can't agree.
hard.fact: Taste and smell combine to create your overall perception of flavor.
hard.q: Why might food taste different when your nose is stuffy?
options: Taste and smell work together for flavor
